paragraphs.text: This is an informal note by Chris Olah exploring how "distributed representations" — a classic idea where information is spread across many neurons rather than one — relates to an idea called superposition. It argues that "distributed representations" actually hides two different strategies, which the note calls composition and superposition.

This matters because breaking a network's representations into separate, independent pieces is what lets researchers understand them at all. Without that split, the number of possible combinations to check grows explosively, a problem the note calls the curse of dimensionality.

Composition means building things from separate, reusable features, like color and shape, so a few features can combine into many stimuli and learning about one combination helps with others. Superposition means packing more things into fewer neurons than you'd expect by overlapping them, letting a small set of neurons store far more items, but you can no longer cleanly pick out a single feature with a simple straight-line test.

The note argues these two strategies actually compete for the same limited space: freely combining features needs room that grows explosively with the number of features, while superposition only works when features rarely combine at once. The two can be partly mixed when combinations are rare, but the note stresses they trade off against each other and should not be confused.

fuller.text: This is an informal note by Chris Olah, published May 4, 2023, about how a classic idea called "distributed representations" relates to something the author calls "superposition." Distributed representations are a way neurons might encode information by spreading it across many of them, rather than using one neuron per idea. The note argues that this classic idea actually bundles together two different strategies, which the author separates and compares.

The author says this distinction matters because breaking down a network's internal representations into separate, independent pieces is necessary to avoid getting overwhelmed by sheer complexity, and to actually understand how neural networks work inside.

Using simple examples of neurons representing colored shapes, the piece contrasts two strategies. "Composition" means separate neurons stand for independent features, like color and shape, which combine to represent objects; this needs few neurons, generalizes well to new combinations, and stays easy to interpret. "Superposition" means a code packs far more items than it has neurons, like bits encoding numbers, but then you cannot cleanly pull out individual features, and in-between or blended objects cannot be represented.

The piece argues these two strategies are actually in tension: fully composable features need exponentially more room as you add features, while superposition only works by giving up composition. Still, the two can partly mix, since features are often sparse, meaning few combinations actually occur, which leaves gaps that can hold additional features in superposition. The author concludes that keeping composition and superposition distinct matters because only composition lets representations be understood with a manageable, non-exploding number of parts.

brief.text: This is an informal note by Chris Olah about how neurons can represent many things at once. It looks at a classic idea called 'distributed representations,' using examples of neurons standing for different colored shapes.

The note says this matters because understanding how representations are built helps us truly understand neural networks. Otherwise, there are too many possible combinations to untangle. The note calls this the curse of dimensionality.

It argues 'distributed representations' really mix two different tricks. 'Composition' combines separate features, like color and shape, so a few neurons can stand for many combinations. 'Superposition' squeezes even more things into very few neurons by overlapping them. But then you need extra work to tell them apart. The note says these two tricks compete: using more of one leaves less room for the other.
